expected_concepts: Establish the foundational visual framework. Define the 2D Cartesian plane with standard basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Emphasize that vectors are arrows from the origin, and points are coordinates. This sets the stage for 'moving' objects.

Define a linear transformation as a function that maps vectors to vectors while preserving two key properties: addition (T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v)) and scalar multiplication (T(cu) = cT(u)). Crucially, explain that the origin (0,0) must always map to itself. Visually, this means the grid lines remain straight and parallel; they do not curve.

Introduce the core insight: To fully describe a linear transformation, you only need to know where the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat end up. Since any vector is a combination of i-hat and j-hat, if you know the new locations of the basis vectors, you know where every other vector goes. This reduces an infinite amount of information to just four numbers.

Connect the geometric movement to algebraic notation. Explain that the matrix is simply a container for the coordinates of the new basis vectors. The first column of the matrix is the new coordinates of i-hat, and the second column is the new coordinates of j-hat. Show how multiplying the matrix by a vector performs the linear combination to find the new vector position.

Apply the concept to a familiar operation: Rotation. Demonstrate that a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation is a linear transformation. Show how i-hat moves to where j-hat was, and j-hat moves to the negative x-axis. Construct the rotation matrix from these new basis positions and verify it works on a test vector.
expected_visual_elements: Visual: A clean, animated grid appears. The x-axis and y-axis are highlighted. Two glowing arrows labeled 'i-hat' and 'j-hat' pulse at the unit marks on the axes. A small robot character stands at the origin (0,0), ready for a journey.

Visual: A 'distortion field' is applied to the grid. The grid lines stretch and shear, but they remain straight and evenly spaced. The robot at the origin stays put. A counter-contrast shows a non-linear transformation where the grid curves, labeled 'Not Linear' in red.

Visual: The robot picks up the i-hat arrow and drags it to a new location (e.g., 2,1). Then it drags the j-hat arrow to another location (e.g., -1,1). As the basis vectors move, the entire grid warps in real-time to follow them. A vector v = 3i + 2j is shown moving from its original spot to its new calculated spot.

Visual: Two boxes appear on the side. Box 1 (Column 1) fills with the coordinates of the moved i-hat. Box 2 (Column 2) fills with the coordinates of the moved j-hat. These two boxes merge into a 2x2 matrix [ [2, -1], [1, 1] ]. An equation appears: Matrix * [x, y]^T = [new_x, new_y]^T, showing the calculation in sync with the grid animation.

Visual: A cartoon cat character sits at a point (1,1). The user selects 'Rotate 90 CCW'. The grid rotates smoothly. The i-hat arrow swings to (0,1) and j-hat swings to (-1,0). The matrix updates to [ [0, -1], [1, 0] ]. The cat character moves from (1,1) to (-1,1), confirming the transformation. The screen flashes 'Transformation Complete!'

author_outline.topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Change
author_outline.target_audience: University students (Undergraduate level, Linear Algebra course)

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Coordinate Grid
sections.content: Establish the foundational visual framework. Define the 2D Cartesian plane with standard basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1). Emphasize that vectors are arrows from the origin, and points are coordinates. This sets the stage for 'moving' objects.
sections.example: Visual: A clean, animated grid appears. The x-axis and y-axis are highlighted. Two glowing arrows labeled 'i-hat' and 'j-hat' pulse at the unit marks on the axes. A small robot character stands at the origin (0,0), ready for a journey.

sections.title: What is a Linear Transformation?
sections.content: Define a linear transformation as a function that maps vectors to vectors while preserving two key properties: addition (T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v)) and scalar multiplication (T(cu) = cT(u)). Crucially, explain that the origin (0,0) must always map to itself. Visually, this means the grid lines remain straight and parallel; they do not curve.
sections.example: Visual: A 'distortion field' is applied to the grid. The grid lines stretch and shear, but they remain straight and evenly spaced. The robot at the origin stays put. A counter-contrast shows a non-linear transformation where the grid curves, labeled 'Not Linear' in red.

sections.title: The Power of Basis Vectors
sections.content: Introduce the core insight: To fully describe a linear transformation, you only need to know where the basis vectors i-hat and j-hat end up. Since any vector is a combination of i-hat and j-hat, if you know the new locations of the basis vectors, you know where every other vector goes. This reduces an infinite amount of information to just four numbers.
sections.example: Visual: The robot picks up the i-hat arrow and drags it to a new location (e.g., 2,1). Then it drags the j-hat arrow to another location (e.g., -1,1). As the basis vectors move, the entire grid warps in real-time to follow them. A vector v = 3i + 2j is shown moving from its original spot to its new calculated spot.

sections.title: Matrices as Transformation Containers
sections.content: Connect the geometric movement to algebraic notation. Explain that the matrix is simply a container for the coordinates of the new basis vectors. The first column of the matrix is the new coordinates of i-hat, and the second column is the new coordinates of j-hat. Show how multiplying the matrix by a vector performs the linear combination to find the new vector position.
sections.example: Visual: Two boxes appear on the side. Box 1 (Column 1) fills with the coordinates of the moved i-hat. Box 2 (Column 2) fills with the coordinates of the moved j-hat. These two boxes merge into a 2x2 matrix [ [2, -1], [1, 1] ]. An equation appears: Matrix * [x, y]^T = [new_x, new_y]^T, showing the calculation in sync with the grid animation.

sections.title: Application: Rotating a Character
sections.content: Apply the concept to a familiar operation: Rotation. Demonstrate that a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation is a linear transformation. Show how i-hat moves to where j-hat was, and j-hat moves to the negative x-axis. Construct the rotation matrix from these new basis positions and verify it works on a test vector.
sections.example: Visual: A cartoon cat character sits at a point (1,1). The user selects 'Rotate 90 CCW'. The grid rotates smoothly. The i-hat arrow swings to (0,1) and j-hat swings to (-1,0). The matrix updates to [ [0, -1], [1, 0] ]. The cat character moves from (1,1) to (-1,1), confirming the transformation. The screen flashes 'Transformation Complete!'

sections.title: Sec 1: Prerequisite: The Coordinate Grid
animations: Animation step 1: Fade in a light gray (#E0E0E0) Cartesian grid on black (#000000) background. Highlight x and y axes in white (#FFFFFF).
Animation step 2: Draw a glowing cyan (#00FFFF) arrow from origin to (1,0). Label it 'i-hat' in cyan.
Animation step 3: Draw a glowing magenta (#FF00FF) arrow from origin to (0,1). Label it 'j-hat' in magenta.
Animation step 4: Pulse both arrows slightly to emphasize their vector nature. Add a small white dot at the origin labeled 'Origin (0,0)' in white.
Animation step 5: Fade in a simple geometric shape (e.g., a triangle) in the first quadrant to represent an object ready for transformation.

sections.title: Sec 2: What is a Linear Transformation?
animations: Animation step 1: Display the formula T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) in white (#FFFFFF) at the top left. Fade it in.
Animation step 2: Animate the grid stretching horizontally. The grid lines remain straight and parallel. The origin dot stays fixed.
Animation step 3: Highlight the origin dot with a yellow (#FFFF00) flash to emphasize it does not move.
Animation step 4: Show a secondary, distorted grid where lines curve. Label it 'Non-Linear' in red (#FF0000).
Animation step 5: Fade out the non-linear grid, leaving only the straight, stretched linear grid to reinforce the concept.

sections.title: Sec 3: The Power of Basis Vectors
animations: Animation step 1: Highlight the i-hat and j-hat arrows with a bright yellow (#FFFF00) glow to indicate they are the key elements.
Animation step 2: Animate the i-hat arrow moving from (1,0) to (2,1). The grid lines attached to the x-axis stretch and shear to follow.
Animation step 3: Animate the j-hat arrow moving from (0,1) to (-1,1). The grid lines attached to the y-axis shear to follow.
Animation step 4: Show a specific vector v = 3i + 2j as a white arrow. Animate it moving to its new position calculated by the new basis.
Animation step 5: Flash the new positions of i-hat and j-hat to show that the entire space has been redefined by these two points.

sections.title: Sec 4: Matrices as Transformation Containers
animations: Animation step 1: Draw two vertical boxes on the right side of the screen. Label them 'Col 1' and 'Col 2' in white.
Animation step 2: Fill 'Col 1' with the coordinates [2, 1] (from i-hat's new position). Color the numbers cyan (#00FFFF).
Animation step 3: Fill 'Col 2' with the coordinates [-1, 1] (from j-hat's new position). Color the numbers magenta (#FF00FF).
Animation step 4: Merge the two columns into a 2x2 matrix bracket. Display the matrix [[2, -1], [1, 1]].
Animation step 5: Show the equation M * v = v' appearing below the matrix, with v' matching the geometric vector position on the grid.

sections.title: Sec 5: Application: Rotating a Character
animations: Animation step 1: Place a simple geometric icon (e.g., a square) at point (1,1) on the grid. Label it 'Object'.
Animation step 2: Animate the entire grid rotating 90 degrees counter-clockwise around the origin. The grid lines remain straight.
Animation step 3: Show i-hat swinging from (1,0) to (0,1). Show j-hat swinging from (0,1) to (-1,0).
Animation step 4: Update the matrix on the side to [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. Highlight the change in white.
Animation step 5: Move the 'Object' from (1,1) to (-1,1). Flash the text 'Transformation Complete!' in green (#00FF00) at the center.
